q: A retailer collects millions of transaction records but none of them are tagged with any target label. Which category of learning algorithm is suited to finding structure in this data?
options: Unsupervised learning
Supervised learning
Reinforcement learning
Semi-supervised learning
explanation: Unsupervised learning finds patterns or structure (such as clusters) in unlabeled data without needing a target variable.

q: An agent that learns to play a game by receiving rewards and penalties for its actions, without being given labeled correct moves, is using ______.
options: Reinforcement learning
Supervised learning from labeled examples
Unsupervised learning
Semi-supervised learning
explanation: Reinforcement learning trains an agent through trial-and-error reward signals rather than labeled examples.

q: A medical imaging lab has a large archive of scans, only a small fraction of which have been labeled by a radiologist as malignant or benign due to the cost of expert review. Which learning paradigm is designed to exploit both the labeled and the much larger unlabeled portion together?
options: Semi-supervised learning
Supervised learning from labeled examples
Unsupervised learning on fully unlabeled data
Reinforcement learning via trial-and-error rewards
explanation: Semi-supervised learning combines a small labeled set with a larger unlabeled set to improve learning beyond what the labeled data alone would allow.

q: Arthur Samuel's 1959 description of machine learning emphasizes that a program should ______.
options: learn without being explicitly programmed for every rule
be evaluated strictly by a task, experience, and performance measure triple
only operate within a reinforcement-learning reward framework
always outperform any hand-coded rule-based expert system on every single task
explanation: Samuel's informal 1959 definition describes machine learning as giving computers the ability to learn without being explicitly programmed.

q: Compared to Arthur Samuel's informal description, what makes Tom Mitchell's 1997 definition of machine learning more rigorous?
options: It explicitly names an experience E, a task T, and a performance measure P that must improve with E
It restricts the definition of machine learning entirely to supervised classification problems trained on labeled data
It was validated empirically across a much larger number of benchmark datasets than Samuel's
It completely removes the need for any performance measure or task definition
explanation: Mitchell's definition is considered more formal because it explicitly decomposes learning into experience (E), task (T), and performance measure (P).

q: A spam filter is said to learn under Tom Mitchell's framework. The task T is classifying emails as spam or not spam, and the performance measure P is classification accuracy on new emails. What plays the role of the experience E?
options: The historical collection of emails the user has previously labeled
The accuracy score computed on new emails after the filter is deployed
The spam-classification task that the filter is being trained to perform
The fixed set of rules a programmer manually hand-codes into the spam filter itself
explanation: In Mitchell's framework, E is the experience the program learns from, which here is the labeled email history used during training.

q: A bank wants to predict whether a loan applicant will default, using a historical dataset where each past applicant is already tagged with 'defaulted' or 'repaid'. This is an example of ______.
options: Supervised learning
Unsupervised learning
Reinforcement learning
Semi-supervised learning
explanation: Because each training example already carries a known target label, this is a supervised learning problem.

q: Predicting a continuous output such as a house price is an example of a ______ problem, while predicting a discrete category such as spam/not-spam is a ______ problem.
options: regression; classification
classification task; regression task
supervised; unsupervised learning
unsupervised; supervised learning
explanation: Regression problems output a continuous numeric value, while classification problems output one of a fixed set of discrete categories.

q: Clustering customers into unnamed segments based on purchasing behavior, with no predefined segment labels, falls under which of the unsupervised learning's typical tasks?
options: Grouping similar data points together without predefined labels
Predicting a numeric target from a labeled training set
Learning a policy through trial-and-error reward signals
Refining labels using a small labeled subset plus a large unlabeled one
explanation: Clustering is a core unsupervised learning task: grouping similar examples together without any predefined category labels.

q: A manufacturing plant wants to flag unusual sensor readings that differ from normal operating patterns, without having any examples of past failures labeled. This task is best framed as ______.
options: Anomaly/novelty detection, an unsupervised learning task
A supervised classification task using failure labels
A reinforcement learning task with a reward for each sensor reading
A semi-supervised task requiring at least some positive failure examples
explanation: Without any labeled failure examples, detecting unusual readings is naturally framed as unsupervised anomaly detection.

q: Why is 'ML is just applying standard programming techniques to solve any problem' a misleading description of machine learning?
options: Machine learning lets the model learn its own rules/parameters from data, not hand-coded
Because all machine learning models inherently execute faster than equivalent hand-written code
Because machine learning never requires any code to be written at all, even for deployment
Because machine learning can only ever be applied to image and text data, never structured data
explanation: The defining feature of machine learning is that the system learns its own internal rules/parameters from data, rather than having every rule explicitly programmed.

q: A self-driving car agent that updates its driving policy based on positive rewards for staying in lane and penalties for collisions is an instance of ______.
options: Reinforcement learning
Supervised learning from labeled driving examples
Unsupervised learning
Semi-supervised learning
explanation: Learning a policy from rewards and penalties through interaction with an environment is the defining feature of reinforcement learning.

q: Which statement correctly distinguishes regression from classification tasks in supervised learning?
options: Regression predicts a continuous numeric value, while classification predicts one of a discrete set of categories
Regression predicts discrete categories, while classification predicts continuous numeric values, the reverse of the truth
Regression requires labeled data, while classification never requires any labels at all
Regression can only ever use exactly one single input feature, while classification can use many
explanation: Regression outputs continuous numeric values; classification outputs discrete category labels. Both are supervised learning tasks and both can use labeled data with any number of features.

q: A hospital has thousands of patient records with lab results but no information about whether each patient was later diagnosed with the condition under study. The hospital wants to discover whether its patients naturally form distinct risk groups. This objective is best achieved with ______.
options: An unsupervised clustering approach
A supervised regression approach
A reinforcement learning approach
A semi-supervised approach requiring at least partial diagnosis labels
explanation: With no outcome labels available, discovering natural groupings in the data is an unsupervised clustering problem.

q: In the univariate linear regression model f(w,b)(x) = wx + b, what do the parameters w and b represent?
options: w is the weight (slope) applied to the input feature, and b is the bias (intercept) term
w is the total number of training examples used, and b is the batch size used during each training step
w is the learning rate controlling the gradient descent step size, and b is the number of iterations
w is the regularization strength applied to the model, and b is the number of input features used
explanation: w and b are the two learnable parameters of the model: w scales the input feature, and b shifts the output.

q: A linear regression model is fit to predict a house's sale price from its floor area. If the fitted model is price = 150 * area + 20000, what does the value 20000 represent?
options: The predicted price when floor area is zero, i.e. the bias/intercept term
The average sale price computed across every house in the full training dataset
The learning rate value used throughout the gradient descent training process
The total number of training examples originally used to fit this particular model
explanation: The constant term in a linear model is the bias/intercept: the predicted output when all input features are zero.

q: Why is linear regression considered a supervised learning algorithm?
options: It is trained on labeled examples consisting of input features paired with known target values
It groups similar inputs together into clusters without relying on any labeled target values at all
It learns purely through trial-and-error reward and penalty signals from an environment
It requires no training data or labeled examples of any kind whatsoever
explanation: Linear regression fits parameters using training examples that each have a known, labeled target value, which is the hallmark of supervised learning.

q: A single training example in a housing price dataset is represented as (x^(i), y^(i)). What does y^(i) represent?
options: The true/target output value for the i-th training example
The predicted output produced by the model for the i-th example
The index position of the example within the dataset
The weight parameter assigned specifically to the i-th input feature
explanation: y^(i) denotes the actual, observed label for the i-th example, as opposed to f(x^(i)), which is the model's prediction.

q: What is the key difference between the model's prediction f(x) and the training label y for a given example?
options: f(x) is the model's estimated output, while y is the actual observed value from the data
f(x) is always required to equal y exactly once training has fully converged
y is computed directly from f(x) by applying the squared-error cost function
f(x) and y are simply two completely different notations referring to the exact same identical underlying quantity
explanation: f(x) is the model's output given its current parameters, while y is the ground-truth label; the cost function measures the gap between them.

q: A model that assumes the relationship between input and output is a straight line will struggle to fit data where the true relationship is strongly curved. This limitation is a direct consequence of ______.
options: linear regression's restriction to a linear combination of the input features
the use of far too many training examples relative to the number of features used overall
an excessively small learning rate chosen for the gradient descent optimizer
the choice of squared error instead of absolute error as the cost function
explanation: Plain linear regression can only represent straight-line (or hyperplane) relationships, so strongly curved patterns require engineered or polynomial features to capture.

q: In the notation m = number of training examples and n = number of features, what does a dataset with m=500 and n=3 represent?
options: 500 labeled examples, each described by 3 input features
3 labeled training examples, each described by 500 separate input features
500 features collected and recorded over 3 separate time periods
3 separate models, each trained independently on 500 examples
explanation: By convention, m counts training examples (rows) and n counts input features (columns), so m=500, n=3 means 500 examples with 3 features each.

q: A simple linear regression model predicts crop yield from rainfall alone. Adding a second input feature, such as average temperature, turns this into ______.
options: a multiple linear regression model with two input features
a polynomial regression model of degree two using only rainfall
a classification model predicting one of two discrete classes
an unsupervised clustering model grouping data into two clusters
explanation: Using more than one input feature while keeping a linear combination of them is called multiple linear regression.

q: Why can a straight-line model still be useful even when the true relationship between inputs and outputs is only approximately linear?
options: It can approximate a roughly linear trend over the range of interest, trading some accuracy for simplicity
It will always fit the training data perfectly, no matter how nonlinear the true underlying relationship actually is
It completely eliminates the need for any cost function during model training
It guarantees exactly zero error on any dataset given enough training iterations
explanation: A linear model trades some accuracy for simplicity and interpretability, and can still be a reasonable approximation when the true relationship is roughly linear.

q: In linear regression notation, x^(i)_j typically refers to ______.
options: the value of the j-th feature in the i-th training example
the predicted output computed for the j-th training example overall
the i-th weight parameter used within the j-th separate trained model
the learning rate value used at iteration i for feature j specifically
explanation: The subscript j indexes the feature and the superscript (i) indexes the training example, so x^(i)_j is the j-th feature's value for the i-th example.

q: After training, a linear regression model is used to predict the output for a brand-new, unseen input. This step is referred to as ______.
options: Inference/prediction
Gradient descent optimization
Feature scaling and normalization
Regularization penalty term
explanation: Using a trained model to produce outputs for new inputs is called inference or prediction, distinct from the training steps that fit the parameters.

q: A dataset used to fit a linear regression model contains an input feature 'number of bedrooms' and a target 'house price'. Which of these is the dependent variable?
options: House price, since it is the quantity being predicted
Number of bedrooms, since it is the quantity being predicted
Both are equally dependent variables in linear regression
Neither; linear regression has no dependent variable
explanation: The dependent variable (target y) is the quantity the model predicts; the independent variable(s) are the input features used to predict it.

q: What is the main purpose of the cost function J(w,b) in linear regression?
options: To quantify how far predictions are from actual targets, so training minimizes this gap
To measure how many total labeled training examples were originally used to fit the model
To determine exactly how many input features should be included in the model
To directly set the learning rate value used by the gradient descent algorithm
explanation: The cost function measures the discrepancy between predictions and actual labels; training searches for parameters that minimize it.

q: The squared-error cost function used in linear regression computes ______.
options: the average squared difference between predicted and actual values across all examples
the total summed absolute difference between every single predicted and actual value
the single maximum prediction error observed anywhere in the training set
the exact count of training examples where the prediction matches the label with complete precision
explanation: Mean squared error averages the squared difference between each prediction and its true label over all training examples.

q: Why is the squared-error term in the cost function typically divided by 2m rather than just m (where m is the number of training examples)?
options: The factor of 2 cancels the 2 from differentiating the squared term
Dividing the squared error by 2m guarantees the cost function becomes strictly non-convex
It mathematically converts the entire cost function into a valid probability distribution
It deliberately doubles the statistical weight given to outliers in the training data
explanation: Differentiating the squared error brings down a factor of 2; including 1/2 in the cost cancels this, giving a cleaner gradient expression.

q: A model's cost J(w,b) is very high on the training set. What does this most directly indicate?
options: The model's predictions are, on average, far from the actual target values
The model has included far too many irrelevant or redundant input features overall
The learning rate chosen for gradient descent is set far too low
The model will definitely generalize poorly to brand-new unseen data
explanation: A high training cost directly reflects large average prediction error on the training data itself; it does not by itself diagnose the cause or predict generalization.

q: For a fixed value of b, plotting the cost J against different values of w for a linear regression problem typically produces a ______ shaped curve.
options: U-shaped/bowl-shaped (convex)
S-shaped (logistic sigmoid) curve
Flat and constant for all values of w
Jagged with multiple separate local minima
explanation: The squared-error cost for linear regression is convex, producing a single bowl-shaped curve with one global minimum.

q: Why is it desirable that the squared-error cost function for linear regression is convex?
options: A convex function has one global minimum, so gradient descent cannot get stuck in a local minimum
Convexity guarantees the trained model will always have exactly zero bias
Convexity would mean the cost surface has several separate, equally good minima to freely choose between
Convexity completely removes the need to ever choose a learning rate value
explanation: Convexity guarantees a single global minimum, so an appropriately tuned gradient descent will not become trapped in a worse local minimum.

q: In a fraud-detection regression task predicting a risk score, if the squared-error cost function yields a much larger penalty for a prediction that misses the true value by 10 units than one that misses by 2 units, this reflects which property of the squared-error cost?
options: It penalizes larger errors disproportionately more, since the error term is squared
It penalizes every single error by exactly the same fixed proportional fraction of the true target value
It completely ignores both the direction and magnitude of the error entirely
It only ever penalizes errors that exceed the overall mean of the target variable
explanation: Because the error is squared, a miss of 10 contributes 100 to the sum while a miss of 2 contributes only 4, so larger errors are penalized disproportionately.

q: The parameters (w,b) that minimize the cost function J(w,b) for linear regression are the ______.
options: parameters that produce the best-fitting line for the training data under the chosen cost
parameters that make the model's predictions always exactly equal every single training label
parameters that instead maximize the squared-error cost function value
parameters chosen arbitrarily before training begins and never updated at all
explanation: Training seeks the (w,b) that minimizes the cost, which corresponds to the best-fitting line under the squared-error criterion, not necessarily a perfect fit.

q: A 3D plot of J(w,b) against w and b for a linear regression problem resembles ______.
options: a bowl, with one unique point at the bottom corresponding to the minimum cost
an irregular saddle shape containing two completely separate dips in different regions
a completely flat plane containing no minimum at all
a jagged series of many disconnected peaks and valleys
explanation: Because the cost is convex in both parameters jointly, its surface over (w,b) forms a single bowl shape with one minimum.

q: Compared to the mean absolute error (MAE), what is a key practical drawback of using mean squared error (MSE) as a cost function when a dataset contains a few extreme outliers?
options: MSE squares errors, so a few large outliers can dominate the cost and skew the line
MSE becomes completely undefined whenever any outliers are present in the data
MSE completely ignores the effect of outliers since it always normalizes the total by m
MSE can only ever be computed for classification-style problems, never regression
explanation: Because squaring amplifies large errors, MSE is more sensitive to outliers than MAE, which grows only linearly with the error size.

q: Suppose two different candidate models give the exact same squared error on every single training example. What must be true about their cost J?
options: Their cost values J(w,b) must be identical
Their cost values must differ because the models have different parameters
Their cost values can only be compared after convergence
Their cost values are undefined since costs cannot be tied
explanation: Since J is computed entirely from the per-example squared errors, identical per-example errors necessarily give identical cost values, regardless of the underlying parameters.

q: In general, the cost function used during training is evaluated on ______.
options: the training data, since training seeks the parameters that minimize this value
data the model has genuinely never encountered before, used purely to test generalization
entirely randomly generated synthetic data that was never part of training
only a single randomly selected training example used for each pass
explanation: The training cost is computed on the training set, since the optimization process is searching for parameters that minimize error on that data.

q: Why does the cost function J(w,b) depend only on the parameters w and b once the training dataset is fixed?
options: Because w and b are the only learned quantities; the features and labels stay fixed
Because the entire training dataset changes dynamically throughout the training process
Because the cost function is recomputed using an entirely new dataset at every single iteration
Because w and b are themselves fully computed from the cost function before training even starts
explanation: Once the dataset is fixed, the only free variables in J are the model parameters, so J becomes purely a function of w and b.

q: After several iterations of gradient descent, the cost J is observed to increase rather than decrease. What is the most likely cause?
options: The learning rate is too large, causing the updates to overshoot the minimum
The learning rate is too small, causing updates to undershoot the minimum
The cost function being minimized happens to already be convex in overall shape
Feature scaling was properly applied to the data before training began
explanation: An increasing cost during gradient descent is a classic symptom of a learning rate that is too large, causing the updates to overshoot and diverge.

q: What is the general update rule used by gradient descent to adjust a parameter w?
options: w is updated by subtracting the learning rate times the cost's partial derivative
w is updated by simply adding the learning rate multiplied by the raw cost value
w is updated by multiplying its current value by the total number of training examples used
w is updated by replacing it entirely with the average of all previous w values
explanation: The standard gradient descent update is w := w - alpha * (dJ/dw), moving the parameter opposite to the gradient direction.

q: In the gradient descent update rule, why is the partial derivative of the cost function subtracted from the current parameter value rather than added?
options: Subtracting the gradient moves the parameter in the direction that decreases the cost
Subtracting the gradient moves the parameter in the direction that increases the cost fastest
Subtraction is specifically required to keep the parameters from ever becoming negative values
Subtraction guarantees the learning rate always stays within a strictly valid numeric range
explanation: The gradient points in the direction of steepest increase of the cost, so subtracting it moves the parameter toward lower cost.

q: Gradient descent is best described as an algorithm that ______.
options: iteratively adjusts parameters in the direction that reduces the cost function
directly solves for the parameters that minimize cost in one closed-form step
randomly searches throughout the parameter space until the cost happens to decrease
only ever works when the cost function is quadratic in every single parameter
explanation: Gradient descent is an iterative optimization method that repeatedly nudges parameters toward lower cost, rather than solving for the optimum in one step.

q: During gradient descent, all parameters (e.g. w and b) should be updated ______.
options: simultaneously, using old parameter values to compute every update before any change
one at a time: updating w completely before even beginning to compute any update for b
in a completely random order re-chosen at each training iteration
only a single time, right at the very end of training
explanation: Correct gradient descent computes all partial derivatives using the current parameter values and then updates every parameter at the same time.

q: A gradient descent run is stopped after a fixed number of iterations even though the cost is still slowly decreasing. What risk does this stopping rule carry?
options: The algorithm may be stopped before reaching a point close enough to the minimum
The algorithm will have already diverged completely long before reaching that point
The cost function will unexpectedly become non-convex
The learning rate will automatically increase without any manual intervention
explanation: Stopping on a fixed iteration count regardless of the cost trend risks halting training prematurely, before the parameters have converged near the minimum.

q: At the exact minimum of a convex cost function, what is true of the gradient (partial derivative) of the cost with respect to each parameter?
options: It equals zero, so gradient descent makes no further updates
It becomes exactly equal to the learning rate value
It reaches its largest possible magnitude at that exact point
It becomes mathematically undefined exactly at the minimum
explanation: At the minimum of a smooth convex function, the slope in every direction is zero, so the gradient descent update becomes zero and parameters stop changing.

q: Why does gradient descent typically take smaller steps automatically as it approaches the minimum of a convex cost function, even with a fixed learning rate?
options: The gradient's magnitude shrinks near the minimum, so update size shrinks too
The learning rate itself is automatically halved at every single training iteration
The number of available training examples steadily decreases as training proceeds
The cost function's overall shape changes as the algorithm approaches the minimum
explanation: Near a minimum, the slope of a convex cost function flattens out, so the gradient magnitude shrinks and the resulting update step shrinks even with a constant learning rate.

q: Gradient descent is applied to a cost function with multiple local minima. Compared to running it on the convex cost function of linear regression, what additional risk arises?
options: The algorithm can converge to a local minimum instead of the global minimum
The algorithm can no longer compute any valid gradient at any point whatsoever
The learning rate must always be deliberately set to a negative value
The cost function is now guaranteed to diverge no matter what
explanation: Non-convex cost functions can have multiple local minima, so gradient descent may settle into one that is not the global minimum depending on initialization.

q: Which of the following is a correct, high-level description of what one iteration of gradient descent does for linear regression?
options: It computes the gradient of the cost for each parameter and takes a small step opposite to it
It evaluates the cost function at every single possible value of w and b and simply selects the smallest one found
It randomly perturbs the parameters and keeps the perturbation only if the cost happens to drop afterward
It solves the normal equation directly and exactly for the optimal parameters in one closed-form step
explanation: Each gradient descent iteration computes the gradient at the current parameters and takes one small step in the direction that reduces cost.

q: A junior data scientist initializes w and b to zero before training a linear regression model with gradient descent on a convex cost function. What should happen as iterations proceed?
options: The parameters should move steadily toward the cost-minimizing values, given a suitable learning rate
The parameters will remain stuck at exactly zero forever, no matter what learning rate is chosen
The algorithm will immediately diverge off toward infinity purely because of the zero initialization chosen here
The cost function itself will become non-convex purely as a result of the zero initialization
explanation: For a convex cost function like squared error in linear regression, gradient descent will move the parameters toward the minimum from any reasonable starting point, including zero.

q: What role does the learning rate play in the gradient descent update rule?
options: It scales the size of the step taken in the direction of the negative gradient each iteration
It determines exactly how many individual training examples are used in each iteration
It sets the total number of distinct input features that are included in the entire model overall
It decides outright whether the cost function turns out to be convex or non-convex
explanation: The learning rate alpha multiplies the gradient in the update rule, controlling how large a step is taken at each iteration.

q: In an agricultural yield prediction model, gradient descent is run with a fixed learning rate and the cost is monitored every iteration. The cost decreases quickly at first and then decreases more and more slowly before leveling off. What does this pattern indicate?
options: The algorithm is converging, since updates shrink naturally as parameters approach the minimum
The learning rate is set too large and the algorithm is actively diverging away from the minimum
The model is underfitting badly and clearly needs several additional relevant input features
The training data must be re-scaled entirely before the algorithm can proceed any further
explanation: A cost curve that decreases quickly then levels off is the expected, healthy pattern as gradient descent approaches a minimum.

q: Why is gradient descent generally preferred over an exhaustive grid search over all possible (w,b) combinations for training a linear regression model?
options: Gradient descent uses the gradient to move efficiently toward the minimum, unlike an impractical exhaustive grid search
Gradient descent will always locate the exact minimum in precisely one single update step, regardless of the starting point chosen
Grid search cannot mathematically be applied to any convex cost function under any circumstances
Gradient descent does not require any cost function to be defined anywhere in the model
explanation: Grid search over a continuous parameter space is computationally infeasible at fine resolution, while gradient descent uses gradient information to move directly and efficiently toward the minimum.

q: A learning curve plots cost J against the number of gradient descent iterations. If the curve decreases at every single iteration and then flattens out, what does this suggest?
options: Gradient descent is working correctly and has converged, or is very close to convergence
The learning rate is far too large and the algorithm is actively diverging away from a minimum
The model is overfitting the training data despite the cost curve still decreasing steadily
The input features were never scaled at all before training the model using gradient descent
explanation: A monotonically decreasing cost that flattens out is the expected signature of a correctly converging gradient descent run.

q: If a learning curve shows the cost J increasing after some iterations rather than monotonically decreasing, the most likely fix is to ______.
options: reduce the learning rate
increase the learning rate
add more training examples
remove the bias term from the model
explanation: An increasing cost typically signals overshooting caused by too large a learning rate, so reducing it is the standard fix.

q: What is a reasonable automatic convergence test for gradient descent?
options: Declare convergence once the cost J decreases by less than a small threshold epsilon between iterations
Declare convergence immediately as soon as the cost is first observed to decrease even slightly
Declare convergence automatically after exactly one hundred iterations, regardless of the cost trend observed
Declare convergence only once the learning rate itself has fully decayed all the way to zero
explanation: A common automatic convergence check compares the change in cost between iterations to a small threshold epsilon, stopping once improvement becomes negligible.

q: Why is examining a learning curve (cost vs. iteration) often more reliable than picking a fixed iteration count in advance to decide when to stop training?
options: Because the iterations needed vary by problem, the learning curve directly shows whether cost has leveled off
A learning curve entirely removes the need to ever choose a learning rate value at all
A fixed iteration count decided in advance will always converge faster than monitoring the actual learning curve
Learning curves completely eliminate the very possibility of a model overfitting the data
explanation: Because the number of iterations needed varies by problem and learning rate, directly observing whether the cost has flattened is more reliable than guessing a fixed count in advance.

q: A data scientist tries learning rates of 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, and 1.0 while monitoring the cost. At a learning rate of 1.0 the cost oscillates wildly and increases overall. What should be tried next?
options: A smaller learning rate, such as one between 0.01 and 1.0
An even larger learning rate to escape the oscillation
More training examples instead of changing the learning rate
Removing the feature scaling that was previously applied
explanation: Oscillating, increasing cost indicates too large a learning rate; the next step is to try smaller values between the last stable and unstable rates.

q: When tuning the learning rate for gradient descent, a common practical strategy is to ______.
options: Try a range of learning rates spaced by a roughly constant multiplicative factor and compare the resulting curves
Always start out with the single largest learning rate that is mathematically conceivable for solving this particular problem
Use the exact same learning rate value that worked well for a completely unrelated dataset, unchecked
Pick whichever learning rate produces the lowest cost on just the very first single iteration alone
explanation: A practical approach is to sweep a range of learning rates spaced by a roughly constant multiplicative factor and compare how the cost behaves over iterations for each.

q: If the learning rate is set far too small, what is the most likely symptom observed in the learning curve?
options: The cost decreases, but so slowly that an impractically huge number of iterations becomes needed
The cost oscillates wildly up and down forever and ever without ever settling anywhere near a true minimum value
The cost diverges outright to an extremely large value within just a handful of iterations
The cost becomes entirely undefined after only a small handful of training iterations
explanation: A learning rate that is too small still moves the parameters in the right direction but takes very small steps, requiring many more iterations to converge.

q: A learning curve for a credit-risk regression model shows the cost dropping sharply for the first 20 iterations and then staying essentially flat for the next 200. What is the most reasonable interpretation?
options: Gradient descent has likely converged, and further iterations provide little additional benefit
The learning rate chosen for training is far too large and should be reduced immediately before continuing
The model has definitely and significantly overfit the entire training dataset by this point in training
The input features were never scaled at all, which is exactly why the curve flattens out so early
explanation: A sharp initial drop followed by a long flat region is the typical signature of convergence, after which further iterations yield little extra benefit.

q: Why can an overly large learning rate cause gradient descent to diverge even when the cost function is convex?
options: A step too large can overshoot the minimum onto a steeper region, compounding over iterations
A convex cost function can supposedly never be minimized by gradient descent under any learning rate whatsoever
Divergence can only ever occur in practice when the underlying cost function itself is non-convex
A large learning rate supposedly converts the entire cost function into a non-convex one
explanation: Even on a convex surface, a step that is too large can overshoot the minimum onto a steeper part of the curve, and repeating this can make the cost grow without bound.

q: Which statement about choosing the learning rate for gradient descent is correct?
options: Too small wastes computation with needlessly many iterations; too large risks overshoot or divergence
The learning rate truly has no effect at all on whether gradient descent converges, only on total training time
A larger learning rate always converges faster and should therefore always be maximized without any limit at all
The optimal learning rate is always exactly one divided by the total number of training examples available
explanation: The learning rate must be balanced: too small wastes iterations, too large risks overshoot or divergence, so tuning is necessary.

q: A plot of cost versus iteration number for gradient descent is called a ______.
options: learning curve
decision boundary
regularization path
confusion matrix
explanation: A learning curve tracks the cost function's value across training iterations, used to visually judge convergence.

q: Suppose the chosen convergence threshold epsilon is set extremely small (e.g. 10^-10). What is the main practical consequence?
options: Gradient descent may run for many extra iterations chasing negligible improvements in cost
Gradient descent will converge in far fewer iterations than it would with a larger epsilon value
The cost function will unexpectedly become non-convex purely because of the threshold chosen
The learning rate will automatically be increased by the algorithm to compensate for this
explanation: An extremely tight convergence threshold forces the algorithm to keep iterating long after further cost reduction becomes practically negligible.

q: In a churn-prediction regression setup, the cost barely changes between iteration 500 and iteration 501 of gradient descent. Based on this alone, which conclusion is best supported?
options: Training is likely near convergence, though this alone does not guarantee the global minimum
The learning rate currently being used must definitely be set far too large for this problem
The model is almost certainly underfitting the data at this particular stage of training
Feature scaling has definitely not been applied anywhere in this particular training pipeline
explanation: A negligible change between consecutive iterations suggests the algorithm is near convergence, though it does not by itself rule out being stuck near a flat region.

q: Which of these learning-curve shapes would most clearly indicate that the learning rate needs to be reduced?
options: A curve where the cost rises and falls erratically, trending upward overall
A curve that decreases steeply at first and then levels off smoothly afterward
A curve that decreases slowly but steadily throughout the entire training process
A curve that decreases and then stays perfectly flat at a very low value indefinitely
explanation: Erratic, overall-increasing cost is the classic sign of a learning rate that is too large and needs to be reduced.

q: In batch gradient descent applied to linear regression, each single update to the parameters uses ______.
options: every training example in the dataset to compute the gradient
exactly one single randomly chosen training example on every update
a small randomly chosen subset of all the training examples available
only the single most recently added training example in the set
explanation: Batch gradient descent computes the gradient by summing or averaging over the entire training set before making a single update.

q: What is the main practical motivation for using stochastic gradient descent (SGD) instead of batch gradient descent on a very large training set?
options: SGD updates using just one example at a time, cheaper than scanning the full dataset
SGD always converges to a meaningfully lower final cost than batch gradient descent does
SGD entirely removes the need to ever choose a learning rate value for training
SGD guarantees a smoother, perfectly monotonically decreasing cost curve throughout
explanation: SGD's key advantage on large datasets is that each update only requires one example, making updates much cheaper than scanning the full dataset every time.

q: Mini-batch gradient descent is best described as a method that ______.
options: Computes each update using a small subset of examples rather than the full dataset or one example
Computes the gradient using the entire dataset at every single iteration, exactly like batch gradient descent does
Updates parameters only after every single example has been seen a fixed number of times total
Skips the gradient computation entirely and instead uses the raw cost value directly
explanation: Mini-batch gradient descent sits between batch and stochastic gradient descent by using a small subset (mini-batch) of examples per update.

q: Compared to batch gradient descent, why does the cost curve for stochastic gradient descent typically look noisier, bouncing up and down rather than decreasing smoothly?
options: Each update relies on only one example, so the gradient estimate varies a lot example to example
Stochastic gradient descent always uses a learning rate that is exactly ten times larger than normal
Stochastic gradient descent does not actually minimize the cost function at all in practice
The cost function itself becomes entirely non-convex when using stochastic updates instead
explanation: Using a single example per update gives a noisy, high-variance estimate of the true gradient, producing a jumpier cost curve than averaging over the full dataset.

q: A company training a regression model on a dataset of 50 million transactions finds that batch gradient descent is far too slow per iteration. Which alternative is most appropriate to address this?
options: Mini-batch or stochastic gradient descent, which avoid scanning the full dataset every update
Increasing the learning rate until convergence supposedly happens within a single training iteration
Switching to an entirely non-convex cost function for this particular regression task
Removing the bias term entirely from the underlying regression model altogether
explanation: Mini-batch or stochastic gradient descent avoid scanning the entire dataset for every single update, making them far more practical at this scale.

q: One epoch of training refers to ______.
options: one complete pass through the entire training dataset
exactly one single parameter update, regardless of the batch size used
one complete run of the automatic convergence test procedure
one single iteration of hyperparameter tuning overall
explanation: An epoch is defined as one full pass through all the training examples, regardless of how many parameter updates occur within it.

q: What trade-off does mini-batch gradient descent offer compared to the extremes of batch and stochastic gradient descent?
options: It balances cheap frequent updates against the more stable gradients from averaging examples
It completely and entirely eliminates the need for any learning rate to be chosen at all
It guarantees convergence to the true global minimum even for completely non-convex cost functions
It always requires strictly fewer total passes through the data than plain batch gradient descent
explanation: Mini-batch gradient descent balances the cheap, frequent updates of SGD against the more stable gradient estimates obtained by averaging over a batch rather than one example.

q: Why might the cost curve of mini-batch gradient descent never settle to a perfectly flat line, even near convergence?
options: Each mini-batch is a different random sample, so the gradient fluctuates slightly batch to batch
Mini-batch gradient descent cannot mathematically ever be applied to any convex cost function at all
The learning rate increases automatically and without bound as training proceeds further
Mini-batch gradient descent recomputes the entire dataset again at every single iteration
explanation: Because each mini-batch is a different sample, the computed gradient and cost naturally fluctuate slightly even once the parameters are near the minimum.

q: A practitioner wants gradient descent updates that are both computationally cheap per step and reasonably stable, avoiding the extreme noise of single-example updates. Which approach fits this goal best?
options: Mini-batch gradient descent with a moderate batch size
Pure batch gradient descent over the full dataset every step
Pure stochastic gradient descent with batch size one
Running gradient descent with no learning rate at all
explanation: Mini-batch gradient descent with a moderate batch size offers a practical middle ground between the cost-per-step of batch GD and the noise of pure SGD.

q: In batch gradient descent, if the training set size m doubles, what is the most direct consequence for each single parameter update (holding the algorithm otherwise fixed)?
options: Each update becomes more costly, since the gradient is averaged over twice as many examples
Each update becomes noticeably cheaper to compute, since there is now much more data available to average over
The learning rate must automatically and immediately double in response
The cost function abruptly becomes non-convex as a direct result
explanation: Because batch gradient descent processes every training example for each update, doubling m roughly doubles the computational cost of each update.

q: A key difference between stochastic gradient descent and batch gradient descent in terms of convergence behavior is that stochastic gradient descent ______.
options: Tends to wander near the minimum rather than settle exactly on it, due to noisy single-example updates
Always converges in strictly and reliably fewer total iterations than plain batch gradient descent ever does
Cannot ever be used together with a gradually decreasing learning rate schedule
Never converges to any region anywhere close to the true minimum at all
explanation: Because each SGD update is a noisy estimate of the true gradient, the parameters typically wander in a small region around the minimum rather than settling exactly on it.

q: A dataset has two features: house size in square feet (ranging from 500 to 5000) and number of bedrooms (ranging from 1 to 5). Without feature scaling, what problem is likely to occur during gradient descent?
options: The cost function's contours become elongated, causing gradient descent to zig-zag slowly
The cost function abruptly and unexpectedly becomes non-convex as a direct result
The model can no longer learn any bias term whatsoever after this
Gradient descent will actually converge noticeably faster than it would with properly scaled features
explanation: When features have very different ranges, the cost contours stretch along the smaller-range feature, causing gradient descent to zig-zag inefficiently toward the minimum.

q: What is the general goal of feature scaling before applying gradient descent?
options: To bring all features into a similar range so convergence is faster
To completely and entirely remove the need for any cost function during training at all
To convert every continuous input feature into a categorical one instead
To substantially increase the total number of features available to the model
explanation: Feature scaling puts all features on comparable scales, which helps gradient descent take more balanced, efficient steps toward the minimum.

q: Mean normalization rescales a feature by ______.
options: subtracting the feature's mean and dividing by its range (max minus min)
subtracting the feature's minimum value and dividing by its maximum value
multiplying the feature directly by the chosen learning rate value
replacing each value with its overall rank among all training examples
explanation: Mean normalization centers a feature around zero by subtracting its mean, then scales it by dividing by its range (max - min).

q: Z-score normalization (standardization) rescales a feature by ______.
options: subtracting its mean and dividing by its standard deviation
subtracting its minimum value and dividing by its overall range
multiplying it by the total number of available training examples
dividing by the single largest value observed anywhere in the training set
explanation: Z-score standardization subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation, producing a feature with mean 0 and standard deviation 1.

q: A loan default model uses 'annual income' (ranging from $10,000 to $500,000) and 'number of credit inquiries' (ranging from 0 to 10) as features. Why would feature scaling likely help gradient descent here?
options: Income's much larger scale would dominate the gradient updates, making convergence slow and uneven
Feature scaling is strictly required because gradient descent supposedly cannot handle more than one feature at a time
Feature scaling is needed specifically to convert this regression problem into a classification problem
Feature scaling would entirely remove the number of credit inquiries as a useful predictor variable
explanation: With such a large scale mismatch between the two features, gradient descent updates become unbalanced; scaling both features helps convergence happen more evenly and quickly.

q: After feature scaling, a model's learned weights w_j become easier to interpret for comparing feature importance because ______.
options: Features now share a comparable scale, so each weight's size more fairly reflects its effect
Scaling supposedly guarantees that every single weight becomes exactly equal to all the others
Scaling entirely removes the bias term from the trained model
Scaling directly converts the weights into probability values
explanation: When features share a comparable scale, differences in weight magnitude more fairly reflect differences in each feature's contribution, rather than differences in raw units.

q: Which of the following symptoms during gradient descent most directly suggests that feature scaling could help?
options: The learning curve converges extremely slowly despite trying several reasonable learning rates
The learning curve converges smoothly and very quickly within just a small handful of iterations
The model's underlying cost function is found to be strictly convex
The dataset contains only a single solitary input feature overall
explanation: Persistently slow convergence despite reasonable learning rates is a classic sign that unscaled features with very different ranges are skewing the cost surface.

q: Why is it important to scale a new test example using the same mean and range/standard deviation computed from the training set, rather than recomputing them from the test example alone?
options: To keep scaling consistent with what the model learned in training, so predictions stay meaningful
Because test examples apparently do not need any kind of scaling at all
Because recomputing statistics from just a single isolated test example alone is mathematically undefined
Because the cost function itself requires test-set statistics during training
explanation: The model's weights were learned relative to the training set's scaling statistics, so new examples must be scaled the same way for predictions to be meaningful.

q: A feature such as 'number of rooms' ranging from 0 to 10, plotted on the same axis as 'house price' ranging from 100,000 to 900,000, would create contour plots of the cost function that are ______ before scaling.
options: very elongated/skewed, making it harder for gradient descent to move directly toward the minimum
perfectly circular in shape, making gradient descent converge immediately in just one single step
undefined entirely, since the cost cannot be computed at all with unscaled features
identical in every way to the contours obtained after proper scaling
explanation: A large scale mismatch between features stretches the cost contours into narrow ellipses, forcing gradient descent to zig-zag rather than move directly toward the minimum.

q: Which statement correctly compares min-max scaling and z-score standardization?
options: Min-max scaling maps values into a fixed range like [0,1]; z-score standardization uses mean and std dev without a fixed bound
Min-max scaling and z-score standardization are always mathematically guaranteed to produce exactly identical rescaled values in every single case
Z-score standardization strictly requires labeled data, while min-max scaling never does
Min-max scaling can only ever be applied to the target variable, never to any input features
explanation: Min-max scaling maps values into a fixed bounded range, while z-score standardization centers and scales by standard deviation without a guaranteed fixed bound.

q: A dataset has a feature with almost no variation (e.g. every patient's 'number of limbs' value is 2) alongside features with wide variation. What is the likely effect of including this near-constant feature on gradient descent, scaling aside?
options: It contributes little useful gradient signal, since there is almost no variation present
It will cause gradient descent to diverge almost immediately after training even begins
It will unexpectedly dominate the overall cost function far more than any other single feature
It converts the entire task from a regression problem into a classification one entirely
explanation: A feature with almost no variation carries little information for the model to exploit, so it contributes little useful signal regardless of scaling.

q: In practice, feature scaling is typically applied ______.
options: before running gradient descent, as a preprocessing step on the training data
after gradient descent has already fully converged, purely as a post-processing step
only ever applied to the target variable y, and never applied to any input features
only ever needed specifically when using the normal equation instead of gradient descent
explanation: Feature scaling is a preprocessing step applied to input features before training, so that gradient descent operates on well-conditioned data from the start.

q: Why is scaling generally considered unnecessary for a dataset with a single input feature on linear regression?
options: There is no second feature with a different scale to cause gradient imbalance between parameters
A single feature always and necessarily has a range of exactly [0,1] by definition
Scaling can mathematically never ever be computed correctly when there is only one single feature present
Single-feature models supposedly do not use gradient descent at all
explanation: Scale imbalance problems arise from comparing features with very different ranges; with only one feature, there is no such imbalance to correct.

q: A dataset has an income feature in whole dollars (e.g. 45,000) and an age feature in years (e.g. 35). If convergence is slow, which action is most directly aimed at correcting the scale imbalance between these two features?
options: Applying feature scaling (e.g. normalization or standardization) to both features
Increasing the number of training iterations substantially without changing anything else
Switching from a linear regression model to a full classification model
Removing the bias term entirely from the trained model
explanation: Feature scaling directly addresses scale imbalance by bringing both features to comparable ranges, which typically speeds up convergence.

q: A model predicting house price only from floor length and floor width might be improved by engineering a new feature equal to length times width. What is this new feature meant to capture?
options: The total floor area, which may relate more directly to price than length and width alone
The simple average of the two original features, used specifically to reduce the parameter count
The ratio of length to width, used specifically to detect scaling errors
A completely randomly generated feature meant only to regularize the model
explanation: Multiplying length by width creates a floor-area feature, which is often more directly predictive of price than the two dimensions taken separately.

q: What does polynomial regression allow a linear-regression-style model to capture that plain linear regression cannot?
options: Curved, nonlinear relationships, captured via added power features like x^2
Decision boundaries that separate discrete output categories from each other
Clustering structure hidden within completely unlabeled training data
Reward-based sequential decision making carried out over many multiple time steps
explanation: By adding powers of the original features as new inputs, polynomial regression can fit curved relationships while still being fit with linear regression's machinery.

q: A polynomial regression model uses features x, x^2, and x^3 derived from a single original input x. Despite the nonlinear relationship with x, why can this still be fit using the same linear regression machinery (cost function and gradient descent)?
options: The model stays linear in its parameters w1, w2, w3 even though nonlinear in x
Because x^2 and x^3 are always exactly numerically identical to x after scaling
Because gradient descent can never be applied to any nonlinear function
Because the cost function stops being convex once polynomial terms are added
explanation: Polynomial regression is nonlinear in the original feature x but remains a linear combination of its parameters, so the same cost function and gradient descent apply unchanged.

q: When using polynomial features such as x^2 and x^3 alongside the original x, why does feature scaling become especially important?
options: Higher powers of x can span a vastly different numeric range, worsening scale imbalance
Polynomial features automatically and entirely cancel the need for any scaling
Feature scaling cannot mathematically ever be applied to polynomial terms at all
Polynomial regression no longer even uses a cost function, so scaling becomes entirely irrelevant
explanation: Raising a feature to a higher power can dramatically widen its numeric range relative to the original feature, so scaling becomes even more important to keep gradient descent efficient.

q: A retailer wants to predict sales using 'advertising spend' and 'store footfall'. Instead of using these separately, an analyst creates a new feature 'spend per visitor' by dividing spend by footfall. This is an example of ______.
options: feature engineering, creating a new feature from existing ones using domain knowledge
feature scaling, which simply normalizes the numeric range of already-existing features
regularization, which penalizes excessively large model weights
polynomial regression, which adds higher-order powers of a feature
explanation: Deriving a new, domain-motivated feature from existing ones (here, spend divided by footfall) is a standard example of feature engineering.

q: Choosing which engineered features (e.g. interaction terms, ratios, polynomial terms) to include in a regression model primarily relies on ______.
options: domain knowledge and intuition about what is likely predictive, refined through experimentation
a fixed, fully automatic rule that always adds every single possible pairwise product of features
the specific numeric value of the learning rate used during training
the specific programming language chosen to implement the regression model
explanation: Feature engineering is driven by domain knowledge about what transformations are likely to be predictive, refined through experimentation.

q: Why can adding a high-degree polynomial term such as x^6 to a regression model increase the risk of overfitting?
options: High-degree terms add flexibility to bend and fit training noise, not just the true trend
High-degree polynomial terms make the entire cost function non-differentiable everywhere
High-degree polynomial terms always drastically reduce the number of training examples available
High-degree polynomial terms forcibly require the model to use stochastic gradient descent
explanation: Very high-degree polynomial terms add enough flexibility that the model can curve through noisy fluctuations in the training data rather than the general trend, increasing overfitting risk.

q: A relationship between house size and price appears to curve upward for very large houses. Which modeling choice directly addresses this curvature within the linear regression framework?
options: Adding a polynomial feature such as size^2 to let the model fit the curve
Rescaling the size feature down to the fixed range [0,1] only
Switching entirely from batch gradient descent to stochastic gradient descent instead
Reducing the learning rate used throughout the training process
explanation: Adding a polynomial feature like size^2 lets a linear-regression-style model represent curvature that a plain straight line cannot.

q: What risk does engineering a very large number of new features (e.g. many polynomial and interaction terms) introduce, even before considering overfitting?
options: It increases computational cost and the chance that some engineered features are irrelevant or highly correlated with others
It guarantees the cost function becomes non-convex
It removes the need for a bias term in the model
It automatically improves the model's performance on new, unseen data
explanation: Adding many engineered features raises computational cost and the chance of irrelevant or highly correlated features, independent of the separate issue of overfitting.

q: An alternative to adding size^2 as a feature to capture curvature could be to add sqrt(size) instead. What does this illustrate about feature engineering in polynomial-style regression?
options: Different transformations of the same original feature can be tried to find one that best matches the shape of the true relationship
Only even powers of a feature are valid transformations in regression
Square root transformations can never be combined with gradient descent
Feature engineering always requires removing the original untransformed feature
explanation: Feature engineering is exploratory: different transformations of the same original feature (squares, square roots, logs, etc.) can be tried to best match the data's true shape.

q: In polynomial regression, if the data's true relationship with the target is actually a straight line, what will likely happen if a high-degree polynomial (e.g. degree 10) is fit anyway?
options: The model risks overfitting, capturing noise in the training data rather than the true simple linear trend
The model will automatically simplify itself back down to degree 1
The cost function will fail to converge under any learning rate
The model will underfit regardless of how it is trained
explanation: Fitting an unnecessarily high-degree polynomial to data that is actually linear tends to overfit, chasing noise instead of the true simple trend.

q: A key reason engineered features like x^2 need the same feature scaling treatment as any other feature is that ______.
options: gradient descent treats every column of the feature matrix the same way, regardless of whether it was engineered or original
engineered features are not technically considered part of the model's input
scaling only matters for the original, unmodified features
polynomial features are already guaranteed to lie in a small range
explanation: Gradient descent does not distinguish between original and engineered features; any feature with a wide range relative to others can cause the same convergence problems.

q: What best characterizes the difference between feature scaling and feature engineering?
options: Feature scaling changes the numeric range of existing features, while feature engineering creates new features from existing ones
Feature scaling creates new features, while feature engineering changes their numeric range
They are two names for exactly the same preprocessing step
Feature scaling applies only to classification models, while feature engineering applies only to regression models
explanation: Feature scaling rescales existing features into comparable ranges; feature engineering derives new, potentially more predictive features from the existing ones.

q: A regression model achieves high error on both the training set and new unseen data. This situation is best described as ______.
options: underfitting, where the model is too simple to capture the underlying pattern
overfitting, where the model has memorized the training data
ideal convergence, since errors are consistent between sets
a data drift problem caused by changing input distributions
explanation: High error on both training and new data indicates the model is too simple to capture the underlying pattern, i.e. underfitting with high bias.

q: A model achieves near-zero error on the training data but performs much worse on new, unseen data drawn from the same distribution. This is a classic sign of ______.
options: overfitting, where the model has fit the noise and specific quirks of the training set rather than the general pattern
underfitting, where the model is too simple
data drift, where the input distribution has changed over time
a convergence failure in gradient descent
explanation: A large gap between very low training error and much higher error on new data from the same distribution is the textbook signature of overfitting.

q: Which of the following is a direct consequence of underfitting in a regression model?
options: High bias, since the model's assumptions are too restrictive to capture the true relationship even on training data
High variance, since the model's predictions change drastically with small changes in training data
Perfect fit on the training set with poor generalization
A fully converged, near-zero training cost
explanation: Underfitting corresponds to high bias: the model is too restrictive to capture the true relationship, leading to high error even on the training data itself.

q: A high-degree polynomial regression model is fit to a small training set and achieves extremely low training error, but its predicted curve swings wildly between data points. This behavior is characteristic of ______.
options: overfitting
underfitting
proper convergence
feature scaling failure
explanation: Extremely low training error combined with wild, erratic swings between data points is a hallmark of overfitting caused by excessive model flexibility.

chart.caption: Figure: a high-degree polynomial fit that swings wildly between training points.

q: Which strategy is commonly used to reduce overfitting in a regression model?
options: Collecting more training data, simplifying the model, or applying regularization
Increasing the polynomial degree further
Removing feature scaling
Decreasing the number of training examples
explanation: Common remedies for overfitting include gathering more training data, simplifying the model (e.g. lowering polynomial degree or dropping features), or adding regularization.

q: A straight-line model is fit to data that is clearly curved, and the resulting fit misses the trend both on training data and new data. What term describes this model's problem?
options: Underfitting / high bias
Overfitting / high variance
Data drift
Label noise
explanation: A model that misses the clear trend on both training and new data, due to being too restrictive, is underfitting and suffers from high bias.

chart.caption: Figure: a straight line fit to clearly curved data.

q: Why is a model that perfectly memorizes every training example not necessarily a good model?
options: It may have simply fit the noise specific to that training set, and so may generalize poorly to new examples
Perfect memorization is mathematically impossible for any regression model
It guarantees the model has zero bias and zero variance simultaneously
It means the model used too few features
explanation: Perfectly memorizing the training set often means the model has fit noise and idiosyncrasies specific to that sample, which can hurt performance on new data.

q: A model with the right balance of complexity for a given dataset is generally expected to achieve ______.
options: low error on the training set and similarly low error on new, unseen data
zero error on the training set and much higher error on new data
high error on both the training set and new data
zero error on new data and high error on the training set
explanation: A well-balanced model generalizes well, achieving low error on both the training set and new data, without the large gap seen in overfitting.

chart.caption: Figure: a model whose fit tracks the underlying trend without chasing noise.

q: Comparing a degree-1 (linear), degree-4, and degree-15 polynomial fit to the same moderately curved dataset, which is most likely to overfit?
options: The degree-15 polynomial, since its high flexibility lets it fit noise in addition to the underlying trend
The degree-1 linear fit, since straight lines always overfit curved data
The degree-4 polynomial, since it is the most balanced choice regardless of the data
All three fits are equally likely to overfit
explanation: The highest-degree polynomial has the most flexibility and is most prone to fitting noise in the training data rather than the general trend.

q: In a manufacturing quality-control model, training error is low but error on next month's production batches is substantially higher, even though the batches come from the same process. Which issue does this most likely reflect?
options: Overfitting to the original training data
Underfitting due to an overly simple model
A reduction in the number of input features
An excessively small learning rate during training
explanation: A large gap between low training error and higher error on new, similarly-distributed batches points to overfitting on the original training set.

q: Which of the following modeling choices would most likely reduce underfitting in a regression model that currently has high error on both training and test data?
options: Adding more relevant features or increasing model complexity (e.g. a higher-degree polynomial term where justified)
Reducing the number of training examples
Increasing the regularization strength further
Removing informative input features
explanation: Underfitting is addressed by increasing the model's capacity to capture the underlying relationship, such as adding relevant features or appropriate higher-order terms.

q: A simple linear model and a complex high-degree polynomial model are both fit to the same dataset. The linear model has higher error on the training set but similar error to the polynomial model on new data. What does this suggest about the polynomial model?
options: The polynomial model is likely overfitting, trading improved training fit for little or no real generalization benefit
The polynomial model is clearly the better choice for deployment
The linear model must have a bug in its cost function
The polynomial model has lower variance than the linear model
explanation: If the more complex model's advantage on training data does not carry over to new data, it is likely overfitting rather than genuinely capturing a better underlying pattern.

q: What is the key practical reason that test or validation performance, rather than training performance alone, should be used to judge whether a model overfits?
options: Training performance alone cannot reveal whether the model has merely memorized the training data instead of learning a generalizable pattern
Training performance is always higher than test performance, regardless of overfitting
Test performance is computed using a different cost function than training performance
Validation data removes the need for a cost function altogether
explanation: Because overfitting means the model does well on training data for the wrong reasons, performance on held-out data is needed to reveal whether it actually generalizes.

q: A dataset is split into a training set and a held-out set that the model never sees during fitting. Comparing error on both sets is primarily useful for ______.
options: diagnosing whether the model overfits (generalizes poorly) or underfits (performs poorly everywhere)
choosing the number of training examples to collect
determining the learning rate to use for gradient descent
deciding whether feature scaling is required
explanation: Comparing training and held-out error is the standard way to diagnose overfitting (large gap) versus underfitting (both errors high).

q: A model with high bias is best described as one that ______.
options: makes overly simplistic assumptions, causing it to systematically miss the true underlying relationship
changes drastically in its predictions when trained on slightly different data
perfectly fits every training example without error
has too many parameters relative to the amount of training data
explanation: High bias arises from a model that is too simple or makes assumptions that are too restrictive, so it systematically underfits the true pattern.

q: A model with high variance is best described as one that ______.
options: is highly sensitive to the specific training data used, producing very different fits if retrained on a different sample
consistently underpredicts the target regardless of the training data used
ignores most of the input features when making predictions
always converges to the same global minimum regardless of initialization
explanation: High variance describes a model whose fitted parameters and predictions change a great deal depending on which particular training sample it saw.

q: The bias-variance tradeoff describes the general observation that ______.
options: reducing a model's bias (by increasing its complexity) tends to increase its variance, and vice versa
bias and variance always increase or decrease together in the same direction
bias only applies to classification models while variance only applies to regression models
increasing model complexity always reduces both bias and variance simultaneously
explanation: The classic tradeoff is that increasing model complexity to reduce bias typically increases sensitivity to the training sample, raising variance, and vice versa.

q: As the degree of a polynomial regression model increases from 1 to a very high value, what typically happens to bias and variance?
options: Bias tends to decrease while variance tends to increase
Bias tends to increase while variance tends to decrease
Both bias and variance tend to decrease together
Both bias and variance remain constant regardless of degree
explanation: Higher-degree polynomials can fit the training data more closely (lower bias) but become increasingly sensitive to the particular training sample (higher variance).

q: A healthcare risk model with very high bias is deployed. Even on the training data used to fit it, its predictions are consistently far from the true outcomes. Which action is most directly aimed at reducing this bias?
options: Increasing model complexity, for example by adding more relevant features or using a higher-degree polynomial
Collecting more training examples using the exact same simple model
Increasing the regularization strength further
Reducing the learning rate used during training
explanation: High bias stems from a model that is too restrictive; increasing its capacity, for example with more relevant features, directly addresses this.

q: Why does simply collecting more training data tend to help a high-variance model more than a high-bias model?
options: More data constrains a flexible, high-variance model to fit the general pattern rather than the noise, whereas a high-bias model is fundamentally too simple to capture the pattern no matter how much data is added
More data always increases bias regardless of model type
A high-bias model always needs less data than a high-variance model
More training data has no effect on either bias or variance
explanation: More data helps a flexible model average out noise and better reveal the true pattern (reducing variance), but it cannot fix a model whose assumptions are fundamentally too restrictive (bias).

q: A model achieves low training error but noticeably higher error on a held-out validation set. In terms of the bias-variance framework, this pattern is most consistent with ______.
options: low bias but high variance
high bias but low variance
both low bias and low variance
both high bias and high variance
explanation: Low training error paired with much higher validation error is the classic signature of low bias (fits training well) combined with high variance (poor generalization).

q: A model achieves high error on both training and validation sets, with the two errors being close to each other. In terms of the bias-variance framework, this pattern is most consistent with ______.
options: high bias and relatively low variance
low bias and high variance
low bias and low variance
high bias and high variance, with both errors differing substantially
explanation: High, similar error on both sets reflects a model too simple to fit even the training data well (high bias) but consistent across samples (low variance).

q: The 'sweet spot' in the bias-variance tradeoff for a given problem refers to ______.
options: the level of model complexity that minimizes overall error on new data by balancing bias and variance
the point where training error first reaches exactly zero
the model with the highest possible number of features
the smallest learning rate that still lets gradient descent converge
explanation: The sweet spot is the complexity level that best balances underfitting and overfitting, minimizing expected error on new data.

q: In a plot of training error and validation error against model complexity, which pattern is expected if the model is suffering mainly from high variance?
options: Training error is low, while validation error is noticeably higher, and the gap between them is large
Both training and validation error are high and close together
Both training and validation error are low and close together
Training error is high while validation error is low
