explanation: High variance is reflected by a large gap between low training error and higher validation error, since the model fits training data well but fails to generalize.

q: A fraud-detection model with extremely high variance is retrained several times, each time on a different random sample drawn from the same larger dataset. What outcome would be expected?
options: The fitted parameters and predictions would differ substantially between retrainings
The fitted parameters and predictions would stay nearly identical between retrainings
The training error would differ substantially while predictions stay the same
The model would consistently underfit across all retrainings
explanation: By definition, a high-variance model is highly sensitive to which particular sample it was trained on, so retraining on different samples would yield substantially different fits.

q: Why is reducing bias and reducing variance often described as competing goals rather than complementary ones?
options: Techniques that make a model more flexible to reduce bias (e.g. adding features, increasing polynomial degree) typically also make it more sensitive to the specific training sample, increasing variance
Because bias and variance are mathematically the exact same quantity measured differently
Because reducing bias always requires reducing the number of training examples
Because variance can only be reduced by increasing the learning rate
explanation: Increasing model flexibility to reduce bias generally increases sensitivity to the particular training sample, which raises variance, making the two goals competing in practice.

q: A regularized linear regression model is compared to the same model without regularization, both trained on identical data. If regularization is set appropriately (not too strong), what is the expected effect on variance?
options: Variance tends to decrease, since regularization discourages the model from fitting noise with overly large parameter values
Variance tends to increase, since regularization adds more parameters to the model
Bias tends to decrease to zero regardless of regularization strength
Neither bias nor variance is affected by regularization
explanation: Appropriately applied regularization discourages large parameter values that often arise from fitting noise, which tends to reduce variance.

q: Which single description best distinguishes bias from variance in a regression model?
options: Bias is error from overly simplistic assumptions about the data; variance is error from excessive sensitivity to the particular training sample
Bias is error only on the test set; variance is error only on the training set
Bias and variance both measure the exact same error and differ only in units
Bias is caused by too much data; variance is caused by too little data
explanation: Bias reflects systematic error from overly simple assumptions; variance reflects how much predictions would change if trained on a different sample.

q: What is the general purpose of adding a regularization term to the cost function of a linear regression model?
options: To discourage overly large parameter values, which helps reduce overfitting
To increase the model's flexibility so it can fit more complex patterns
To replace the need for a learning rate during gradient descent
To guarantee the model achieves zero training error
explanation: Regularization adds a penalty for large weights to the cost function, discouraging the model from relying too heavily on any one feature and helping reduce overfitting.

q: In regularized linear regression, the regularization term is typically added as a penalty based on ______.
options: the size (e.g. squared magnitude) of the model's weight parameters
the number of training examples used
the value of the learning rate
the number of iterations gradient descent has run
explanation: The regularization penalty is typically the sum of squared weights (or similar), scaled by a regularization strength, discouraging large parameter values.

q: What effect does increasing the regularization strength (often called lambda) have on a linear regression model's fitted weights, all else equal?
options: It shrinks the weights toward smaller values, reducing the model's sensitivity to individual features
It increases the weights, making the model more sensitive to individual features
It has no effect on the weights, only on the bias term
It converts the weights into probabilities
explanation: A larger regularization strength more heavily penalizes large weights, shrinking them toward smaller values and reducing sensitivity to any single feature.

q: If the regularization strength lambda is set far too high in a regularized regression model, what is the most likely outcome?
options: The weights are pushed so close to zero that the model underfits, barely reacting to the input features
The model will overfit even more severely than without regularization
The cost function will become non-convex
The learning rate will automatically increase to compensate
explanation: Excessive regularization shrinks weights so aggressively toward zero that the model loses the ability to react to the input features, causing underfitting.

q: A high-degree polynomial regression model is overfitting a small training set. Besides reducing model complexity or gathering more data, what is another common way to address this?
options: Apply regularization to penalize large weights without removing the higher-order features entirely
Increase the learning rate until the training cost reaches zero
Switch exclusively to stochastic gradient descent
Remove feature scaling from the pipeline
explanation: Regularization offers a middle path: it keeps the higher-order features in the model but discourages them from taking on extreme values that cause overfitting.

q: Why is the bias term b typically excluded from the regularization penalty in regularized linear regression?
options: The bias simply shifts the model's output and does not contribute to the overfitting caused by large feature weights, so convention leaves it unpenalized
Including the bias in the penalty would make the cost function undefined
The bias term is always exactly zero in regularized models
Regularization cannot mathematically be applied to any additive constant
explanation: Because the bias term only shifts predictions rather than scaling any feature, it is conventionally left out of the regularization penalty, which targets the weights.

q: Setting the regularization strength lambda to exactly zero in a regularized linear regression model is equivalent to ______.
options: ordinary (unregularized) linear regression
a model that ignores all input features
a model that can no longer be trained using gradient descent
a model guaranteed to overfit regardless of its complexity
explanation: With lambda set to zero, the regularization penalty vanishes and the cost function reduces to the ordinary squared-error cost of unregularized linear regression.

q: A credit scoring model regularizes its weights to prevent a small number of unusual applicants in the training data from having an outsized effect on the fitted parameters. This illustrates regularization's role in ______.
options: reducing variance by discouraging the model from fitting noise or idiosyncrasies in the training sample
reducing bias by making the model more flexible
increasing the number of features automatically
guaranteeing convergence in a single gradient descent iteration
explanation: By discouraging large weights driven by a few unusual examples, regularization reduces the model's sensitivity to the particular training sample, i.e. reduces variance.

q: Choosing an appropriate regularization strength lambda typically involves ______.
options: trying a range of values and comparing performance on a validation set to find a good balance between bias and variance
always setting lambda as large as mathematically possible
setting lambda equal to the learning rate used in gradient descent
setting lambda equal to the number of training examples
explanation: Lambda is typically tuned by trying several candidate values and comparing validation performance to find a good tradeoff between underfitting and overfitting.

q: How does the gradient descent update rule change when a regularization term is added to the cost function, compared to unregularized linear regression?
options: An extra term proportional to the weight itself (scaled by lambda) is added to the gradient, which shrinks the weight slightly at every update
The update rule is identical, since regularization only changes the final reported cost, not the gradient
The learning rate is automatically replaced by lambda
The update rule skips the bias term's gradient entirely, even without regularization
explanation: Adding a weight-penalty term to the cost introduces an additional gradient term proportional to the weight, which causes each update to also shrink the weight slightly.

q: Which scenario would benefit most from increasing regularization strength?
options: A high-degree polynomial model that fits the training data almost perfectly but performs much worse on validation data
A simple linear model that performs poorly on both training and validation data
A model whose training and validation errors are both low and close together
A model that has not yet been trained with gradient descent
explanation: A large gap between near-perfect training fit and much worse validation performance signals overfitting, which increased regularization is designed to address.

q: Why is regularization often described as a tool for managing the bias-variance tradeoff rather than purely 'fixing overfitting'?
options: Too little regularization can leave variance high, while too much regularization can introduce excessive bias, so an appropriate middle value must be chosen
Regularization only ever affects bias and never affects variance
Regularization removes the bias-variance tradeoff from consideration entirely
Regularization is only relevant to classification, not regression
explanation: Regularization strength must be tuned carefully: too little leaves variance high (overfitting), while too much introduces excessive bias (underfitting).

q: A dataset with very few training examples relative to the number of features is especially prone to overfitting. Which technique directly helps control this by penalizing complexity rather than requiring additional data?
options: Regularization
Increasing the learning rate
Switching to batch gradient descent from mini-batch
Removing feature scaling
explanation: Regularization controls overfitting by penalizing large weights directly in the cost function, which is especially useful when collecting more data is not feasible.

q: In multiple linear regression with n input features, the model is typically written as f(x) = w1*x1 + w2*x2 + ... + wn*xn + b. What does each wj represent?
options: The weight associated with the j-th feature, reflecting its contribution to the prediction
The value of the j-th training example
The number of iterations used to train the j-th parameter
The regularization strength applied to the j-th feature only
explanation: Each wj scales the contribution of the j-th feature to the model's prediction, analogous to the single weight w in univariate linear regression.

q: Why is vectorized implementation (using matrix/vector operations) generally preferred over writing an explicit loop over features when computing predictions in multiple linear regression?
options: Vectorized operations are typically much faster in practice, since they can exploit optimized numerical libraries and parallel hardware
Vectorized operations always produce a different, more accurate prediction than a loop
A loop-based implementation cannot mathematically compute the same result as a vectorized one
Vectorization removes the need for a cost function
explanation: Vectorized operations compute the same mathematical result as an explicit loop but run much faster in practice by leveraging optimized libraries and hardware parallelism.

q: The normal equation provides a way to find the optimal parameters for linear regression by ______.
options: directly solving a closed-form equation derived from setting the gradient of the cost function to zero, without iterating
iteratively updating parameters using a learning rate, exactly like gradient descent
randomly sampling candidate parameter values until the cost decreases
requiring the features to first be converted into probabilities
explanation: The normal equation solves directly for the parameters that set the cost function's gradient to zero, avoiding the need for iterative updates.

q: What is a key practical limitation of the normal equation compared to gradient descent, especially as the number of features n grows very large?
options: It requires computing a matrix inverse, which becomes computationally expensive as n grows large
It cannot be used for any dataset with more than one feature
It requires choosing a learning rate, unlike gradient descent
It only works correctly when the cost function is non-convex
explanation: The normal equation requires inverting an (n x n) matrix, an operation whose cost grows rapidly as the number of features increases, making it impractical for very large n.

q: Unlike gradient descent, the normal equation does not require ______.
options: choosing a learning rate or iterating repeatedly until convergence
a training dataset of labeled examples
a cost function to be defined at all
any computation of matrix operations
explanation: The normal equation solves for the optimal parameters directly in one step, so unlike gradient descent it needs no learning rate or iterative convergence check.

q: A dataset has n = 10,000 features. Which training approach is generally more practical in this setting?
options: Gradient descent, since the normal equation's matrix inversion step becomes very costly at this scale
The normal equation, since it is always faster regardless of the number of features
Neither approach can be used once n exceeds 1,000 features
Only stochastic gradient descent with batch size equal to n
explanation: With tens of thousands of features, the matrix inversion required by the normal equation becomes very costly, making gradient descent the more practical choice.

q: In multiple linear regression, what does vectorization specifically replace?
options: An explicit for-loop over each feature/weight pair with a single matrix or dot-product operation
The entire cost function with a simplified approximation
The gradient descent update rule with the normal equation
The training labels with predicted values
explanation: Vectorization replaces an explicit loop summing wj*xj terms with a single dot-product (or matrix) operation computing the same result.

q: A dataset has features 'number of bedrooms', 'floor area', 'age of property', and 'distance to city center' used to predict house price. This represents a linear regression problem with how many input features (n)?
explanation: Each listed attribute used as a model input counts as one feature, so there are four input features (n=4) in this example.

q: Why does gradient descent remain useful for linear regression even though the normal equation can solve for the optimal parameters directly in closed form?
options: Gradient descent scales better to problems with a very large number of features and generalizes naturally to other models where no closed-form solution exists
Gradient descent always finds a more accurate solution than the normal equation
The normal equation cannot be applied to any linear regression problem
Gradient descent eliminates the need for a training dataset
explanation: Gradient descent avoids the costly matrix inversion required at scale and extends naturally to other models (e.g. with regularization or nonlinearities) that lack a closed-form solution.

q: When features are represented as a vector x = [x1, x2, ..., xn] and weights as a vector w = [w1, w2, ..., wn], the prediction f(x) = w1x1 + w2x2 + ... + wnxn + b can be computed efficiently as ______.
options: the dot product of w and x, plus the bias b
the elementwise maximum of w and x, plus the bias b
the matrix inverse of w times x
the sum of all elements in x alone, ignoring w
explanation: The weighted sum of feature values is exactly the dot product of the weight vector and feature vector, plus the bias term.

q: A dataset's feature matrix X has one row per training example and one column per feature. If X has 200 rows and 6 columns, what does this represent?
options: 200 training examples, each described by 6 features
6 training examples, each described by 200 features
200 features collected across 6 separate experiments
6 separate models trained on 200 examples each
explanation: By the stated convention, rows correspond to training examples and columns correspond to features, so 200 rows and 6 columns means 200 examples with 6 features each.

q: A dataset has far more features than can comfortably fit in memory for matrix inversion. Which training method avoids the need to invert a large matrix altogether?
options: Gradient descent
The normal equation
Mean normalization
Z-score standardization
explanation: Gradient descent only requires computing gradients at each step and never needs to form or invert a large feature matrix, unlike the normal equation.

q: Gradient descent and the normal equation are both methods for finding the parameters of a linear regression model that ______.
options: minimize the squared-error cost function on the training data
maximize the squared-error cost function on the training data
minimize the number of features used by the model
maximize the learning rate used during training
explanation: Both methods aim at the same goal: finding the parameters (w,b) that minimize the squared-error cost on the training data, just via different computational approaches.
